title: “HEAP BURNING COALS ON HIS HEAD” — DID GOD REALLY TELL YOU TO HURT YOUR ENEMIES WITH KINDNESS?
paragraphs: “HEAP BURNING COALS ON HIS HEAD” — DID GOD REALLY TELL YOU TO HURT YOUR ENEMIES WITH KINDNESS?

The shocking truth behind Romans 12:20 that exposes the difference between Christian love and disguised revenge—and why the people who wounded you may reveal something about the condition of your own heart.
There is a kind of revenge that looks so holy, even Christians can mistake it for obedience.
You smile at someone who betrayed you.
You speak gently to someone who humiliated you.
You help someone who would never lift a finger to help you.
And somewhere deep inside, where nobody else can hear your thoughts, you whisper:
“Just wait. God will make you regret what you did to me.”
You call it kindness.
You call it taking the high road.
You might even quote Scripture to justify it.
“If thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.” — Romans 12:20 (KJV)
There it is.
The verse that sounds like heaven has finally given you permission to burn someone without touching them.
Be kind enough to make them suffer.
Love them until they feel guilty.
Bless them so dramatically that they cannot escape the shame of what they did.
And when they finally break under the weight of your goodness, you can quietly congratulate yourself for obeying God.
But what if that is not what Paul meant?
What if the very Scripture you have been using to justify your secret desire for revenge is actually confronting that desire?
What if those burning coals were never meant to become another weapon in your hands?
And what if the most uncomfortable part of Romans 12:20 is not what God might do to your enemy...
But what He is asking to change inside you?
Because sometimes the person we want God to humble is not the only person who needs to repent.
Sometimes the fire reaches our own hearts first.
If anyone could have justified revenge, it was Him.
Yet the cross tells a radically different story.
To understand why, we have to return to the actual words of Scripture.
Paul writes in Romans 12:19:
Notice what Paul says before he mentions the burning coals.
Do not avenge yourselves.
Not with your fists.
Not with your words.
Not through public humiliation.
Not through carefully arranged acts of kindness designed to make someone feel small.
The Greek word translated “avenge” comes from ekdikeō (ἐκδικέω), meaning to exact justice, avenge, or vindicate.
Paul is not saying injustice is imaginary. He is not telling wounded people to pretend their suffering never happened.
He is telling believers that personal vengeance does not belong in their hands.
Then he quotes the Lord's declaration from Deuteronomy 32:35: “To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence” (KJV).
God is not indifferent to evil.
He sees what happened.
He knows what was said behind your back.
He knows the promises that were broken, the money that was stolen, the lies that damaged your reputation, the trust that was exploited, and the tears you wiped away when nobody was watching.
But God's perfect knowledge of injustice does not give us permission to become instruments of personal revenge.
And then Paul continues:
“Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.” — Romans 12:20 (KJV)
Paul is quoting Proverbs 25:21–22.
This command did not suddenly appear in the New Testament. Its roots reach back into the wisdom literature of ancient Israel.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 25:22 includes these words:
כִּי גֶחָלִים אַתָּה חֹתֶה עַל־רֹאשׁוֹ
Ki geḥalim attah ḥoteh ʿal-rosho.
Literally, the phrase speaks of gathering or heaping burning coals upon his head.
The Hebrew word geḥalim (גֶחָלִים) means burning coals or embers. The verb ḥoteh (חֹתֶה), from ḥātāh, conveys the action of taking up or gathering coals.
In Romans, the corresponding Greek expression is:
ἄνθρακας πυρὸς σωρεύσεις ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ
Anthrakas pyros sōreuseis epi tēn kephalēn autou.
“You will heap burning coals upon his head.”
The Greek verb sōreuō (σωρεύω) means to heap up or pile together.
The image is intense.
Paul does not soften it.
But the crucial question is what the image means within the passage.

Some interpreters understand the burning coals as a picture of painful shame or remorse that may lead an enemy toward repentance. Others emphasize the possibility of divine judgment upon someone who persists in evil despite receiving kindness.

The precise background of the metaphor remains debated. A frequently repeated explanation connects it to an ancient Egyptian repentance ritual involving coals carried on the head, but that specific historical explanation is not firmly established and should not be presented as proven biblical fact.
What we can say with confidence is that neither Proverbs nor Romans authorizes believers to use kindness as a method of psychological torture.
Why?
Because Paul immediately explains the moral direction of his teaching:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.” — Romans 12:21 (KJV)
Overcome evil with good.
Not with disguised evil.
Not with spiritualized cruelty.
Not with a smile concealing the desire to see someone destroyed.
With good.
The Greek word translated “good” is agathos (ἀγαθός), describing what is good in a moral sense.
And the command to overcome evil carries the language of victory.
Paul is calling believers to resist being conquered by evil and to defeat its influence through genuine goodness.
Think about that.
If somebody's hatred turns you into a hateful person, what has happened?
Their evil has begun to shape your character.
If their cruelty teaches you to enjoy cruelty, even when disguised as righteousness, their sin has gained influence over your heart.
If their betrayal makes revenge the organizing purpose of your life, the wound has become a master.
You may have escaped the person.
But have you escaped what their actions are doing inside you?
That is the question Romans 12 refuses to let us avoid.
And it is painful because some of us have been carrying our enemies inside our hearts for years.
You still remember the conversation.
The exact words.
The look on their face.
The moment you realized someone you trusted was capable of hurting you so deeply.
Maybe it was a spouse who shattered your marriage.
A friend who exposed something private.
A church leader who abused spiritual authority.
A relative who treated you like you were disposable.
A business partner who took advantage of your generosity.
Or someone who wounded you and then carried on with life as though nothing happened.
You tried to pray.
You tried to move forward.
You told people you had forgiven them.
But then you saw them smiling in a photograph.
Enjoying success.
Receiving applause.
Being celebrated by people who had no idea what they had done.
And something inside you screamed:
“Lord, how can they be happy after what they did to me?”
That question is more human than many Christians are willing to admit.
Scripture itself contains cries for justice.
The Psalms are filled with wounded people bringing their anguish before God.
Biblical faith does not require emotional dishonesty.
But there is a difference between asking God for justice and demanding that God satisfy our appetite for revenge.
There is a difference between grieving over wickedness and secretly hoping another human being becomes miserable.
And there is a difference between wanting someone to repent and wanting someone to suffer.
Repentance seeks transformation.
Revenge seeks repayment.
The Gospel calls us to surrender vengeance to the only Judge who sees every heart without distortion.
But please understand something equally important.
Forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation.
And kindness does not mean abandoning wisdom.
Romans 12:20 does not require an abused person to return to an unsafe home.
It does not require a victim to conceal a crime.
It does not demand that someone continue lending money to a person who repeatedly exploits them.
It does not mean giving an unrepentant offender unrestricted access to your children, your finances, your home, or your emotional life.
You can forgive while maintaining necessary boundaries.
You can refuse revenge while seeking lawful justice.
You can pray for someone's repentance while reporting wrongdoing to appropriate authorities.
You can love an enemy without pretending that enemy is trustworthy.
Romans 13, immediately following Paul's teaching on overcoming evil, recognizes the legitimate role of governing authorities in restraining and punishing wrongdoing.
The same Bible that commands personal mercy does not erase public justice.
And if you are still in danger, seeking protection is not a failure of Christian love.
It is entirely possible to refuse hatred and still say:
“You cannot keep hurting me.”
That is not revenge.
That is a boundary.
Now consider the greater shock of this passage.
Jesus did not merely command His followers to love enemies.
He lived it.
In Matthew 5:44, He says:
“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.” (KJV)
These words are not permission to manipulate enemies into feeling guilty.
They are a call to reflect the character of our heavenly Father.
Jesus continues by reminding His listeners that God causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good and sends rain upon the just and unjust.
God's generosity exposes how narrow our own love can become.
We are often willing to love those who appreciate us.
We are willing to help those who thank us.
We are willing to forgive those who apologize beautifully.
But what happens when the person does not apologize?
What happens when they never acknowledge the damage?
What happens when your kindness is met with indifference?
What happens when obedience brings no satisfying emotional ending?
Will you still obey Jesus?
That is where love stops being a performance.
That is where the Gospel begins to confront our motives.
Because if your kindness only feels worthwhile when your enemy suffers, you may not be seeking their good at all.
You may simply be looking for a more respectable way to retaliate.
And here is where the story becomes deeply personal.
There was a time when you were not merely someone wounded by sin.
You were also someone guilty of sin.
So was I.
The Bible does not divide humanity into innocent people who need kindness and guilty people who deserve only contempt.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (KJV)
All.
The betrayer and the betrayed.
The offender and the wounded.
That does not make every wrongdoing equally severe. It does not remove the responsibility of those who commit terrible harm.
But it does mean that none of us can stand before a holy God claiming to be righteous through our own merit.
And Romans 5:8 delivers the truth that changes everything:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned up our lives.
Not after we became worthy of His affection.
Not after we apologized perfectly.
Christ died for us while we were still guilty.
Then Romans 5:10 goes further:
“For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.” (KJV)
Did you catch that word?
Enemies.
We were enemies.
And instead of leaving sinners without hope, God acted in love through His Son to make reconciliation possible.
The eternal Son of God took on human flesh.
Jesus lived the righteous life we could never live perfectly.
He bore our sins upon the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
He did not come merely to teach wounded people how to become emotionally stronger.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to break the dominion of sin and death.
He came to give new life to people who could never rescue themselves.
And suddenly Romans 12:20 becomes far more than a lesson about difficult relationships.
It becomes a window into the transforming power of the Gospel.
Because Christians are not called to show mercy in order to earn salvation.
We are called to show mercy because we have received mercy through Jesus Christ.
We do not forgive because sin is harmless.
We forgive because we know what it cost our Savior to deal with sin.
We do not abandon revenge because justice is unimportant.
We abandon personal vengeance because God is perfectly just.
And we do not love enemies because we are naturally better than they are.
We love because Christ first loved us.
Now picture Calvary.
The soldiers have driven nails through the hands and feet of Jesus.
His body is wounded.
His enemies mock Him.
Religious leaders ridicule Him.
People who witnessed His compassion now stand near the cross as He suffers.
The One who healed the sick is being treated as a criminal.
The One who welcomed sinners is being rejected.
The One who never sinned is suffering under the weight of human wickedness.
And Luke 23:34 records Jesus saying:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” (KJV)
This saying is preserved in many ancient manuscripts, although some early witnesses omit it, a textual detail worth acknowledging when studying the passage carefully.
Yet the prayer itself beautifully accords with the mercy Jesus taught throughout His ministry.
He did not celebrate the evil done to Him.
He did not declare His executioners innocent.
He did not pretend the cross was anything other than an act of terrible injustice.
He prayed.
And His prayer revealed a mercy deeper than human instinct.
That mercy did not make repentance unnecessary.
It revealed the heart of the Savior through whom forgiveness is offered.
And perhaps this is what makes the command to love enemies so difficult.
We want our enemies to feel the weight of their sin.
But Jesus also wants us to remember the weight of ours.
We want God to confront what they have done.
And He may.
But He also confronts what we have become while carrying the wound.
We want their hearts to break.
Yet perhaps our own hearts have become hard in places we no longer notice.
Have you ever replayed someone's failure because remembering it made you feel morally superior?
Have you ever imagined the day they would come crawling back, finally admitting that you were right?
Have you ever offered help while secretly hoping your generosity would humiliate them?
Have you ever prayed, “Lord, bless them,” while quietly hoping the blessing would never arrive?
These are uncomfortable questions.
But grace often begins its deepest work where our carefully managed religious image starts to crack.
And maybe you have just recognized yourself.
Not in the betrayal you suffered.
Not in the wrong someone committed against you.
But in the bitterness you have been protecting ever since.
If that is where you are, do not hide behind another spiritual performance.
Come to Christ honestly.
You do not have to call evil good.
You do not have to manufacture feelings you do not possess.
You do not have to pretend the wound has healed.
You can say:
“Lord Jesus, I am still angry.”
“I still want them to understand what they did.”
“Sometimes I want them to hurt the way I hurt.”
“I know You are calling me away from revenge, but I cannot change my heart by pretending.”
“Have mercy on me. Teach me to love without surrendering truth.”
That is not a polished prayer.
But it is an honest one.
And the God who knows your heart already is not impressed by a mask.
He calls you to come into the light.
The Greek word often translated “repentance” is metanoia (μετάνοια), referring to a change of mind or disposition, and in the New Testament it belongs to the larger call to turn from sin toward God.
Repentance is more than feeling bad.
It involves turning.
Turning away from cherished bitterness.
Turning away from the fantasy of revenge.
Turning away from the belief that your enemy's destruction is necessary for your healing.
And turning toward Jesus Christ, who alone can forgive sin and transform the human heart.
This does not mean emotional pain disappears immediately.
Some wounds take time to process.
Some situations require wise counsel, accountability, protection, and patient recovery.
Forgiveness may be a settled commitment that you must repeatedly bring before God when old memories return.
And sometimes the first evidence of change is not that you suddenly feel affection for someone who harmed you.
It is that you stop feeding the desire to destroy them.
You stop rehearsing imaginary revenge.
You stop arranging your goodness as a public accusation.
You stop measuring your freedom by whether they finally admit they were wrong.
You begin to pray for truth.
For justice.
For repentance.
For protection of those who might otherwise be harmed.
And, where possible, for their genuine restoration through Christ.
That is not weakness.
That is what it looks like when the Gospel begins to loosen sin's grip on a wounded heart.
But there is another danger.
Some Christians hear this teaching and immediately turn it into pressure against wounded people.
They say, “You must forgive,” but never confront the person who committed the evil.
They demand reconciliation without repentance.
They tell victims to be silent in order to preserve a church's reputation.
They use biblical language to protect powerful offenders.
That is not what Romans 12 teaches.
Biblical mercy must never become a shelter for ongoing abuse.
Christian love does not rejoice in unrighteousness.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 13:6 that love “rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth” (KJV).
Truth matters.
Accountability matters.
Justice matters.
And sometimes loving an offender means refusing to enable their continued wrongdoing.
Sometimes the most merciful thing you can do is tell the truth and allow legitimate consequences to follow.
The purpose is not revenge.
It is righteousness, protection, and, where God grants it, repentance.
And now we return to those burning coals.
What if your enemy feels ashamed because you refuse to retaliate?
That may happen.
What if your kindness becomes part of what awakens their conscience?
That may happen too.
What if they repent, seek forgiveness, and begin to change?
Praise God.
But what if they do none of those things?
What if they laugh at your kindness?
What if they interpret your mercy as weakness?
What if they never confess?
What if they die without ever telling you they were sorry?
Does that mean your obedience failed?
No.
Because Romans 12:20 is not a promise that your kindness will force repentance.
It is a command governing how you respond to evil.
You cannot control another person's conscience.
You cannot manufacture another person's repentance.
You cannot save someone by being sufficiently kind.
Only God can change the heart, and salvation comes through Jesus Christ.
Your responsibility is not to become the Holy Spirit in somebody else's life.
Your responsibility is to obey the Lord who has shown you mercy.
And that obedience may be unseen.
It may happen when you choose not to publish the humiliating details you know about someone.
When you refuse to return an insult.
When you give truthful testimony without embellishment.
When you stop encouraging others to hate someone on your behalf.
When you pray for an offender's repentance while still maintaining necessary distance.
When you refuse to let bitterness become the inheritance you pass to your children.
These moments may never go viral.
Nobody may applaud them.
Your enemy may never notice.
But your Father sees.
And sometimes the most significant victory is not that your enemy finally admits defeat.
It is that their sin no longer dictates who you are becoming.
This is why the Gospel Warrior message matters so deeply:
Not because every earthly scandal receives a beautiful public resolution.
Not because every broken relationship is restored.
Not because every offender repents.
But because Jesus can redeem sinners, transform lives, sustain the wounded, and give eternal hope even when earthly circumstances remain painfully unfinished.
The cross was the place where human injustice and divine mercy met in a way no human being could have invented.
And the resurrection declared that sin, death, and the grave would not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
Your past does not have to become your identity.
Your wounds do not have to become your master.
Your bitterness does not have to become your future.
And your enemy does not have to become the center of your story.
Jesus Christ is worthy of that place.
Maybe you came into this article looking for permission to make someone regret hurting you.
But now you realize the Lord is inviting you into something far greater than revenge.
Freedom from being ruled by it.
Not freedom from accountability.
Not freedom from consequences.
Not freedom from grief.
But freedom to belong wholeheartedly to Christ, even while healing.
And if this has exposed something you have kept hidden, I want to invite you to respond with spiritual honesty.
You do not need to describe your trauma publicly or reveal the identity of anyone who harmed you. God knows the details you are not ready to share.
Someone reading may desperately need to know that God's grace is not a theory.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this truth.
Perhaps they are angry at a former spouse.
Perhaps they are quietly planning revenge against someone who betrayed them.
Perhaps they have confused forgiveness with returning to danger.
Or perhaps they are the person who has caused harm and desperately needs to repent.
Because the next time anger rises, you may need to remember that overcoming evil with good is not the same as pretending evil never happened.
Every soul matters.
Every opportunity to make the Gospel known matters.
And there is something else I want to share with you.
Gospel Warrior is not meant to be merely another page that fills your feed with religious words.
Our desire is to help people encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in biblical discernment, turn from sin, find encouragement in Christ, and become more deeply rooted in the Word of God.
We want biblical nourishment to reach people who may not be able to afford shelves full of Christian books.
We want believers to have resources they can return to when their faith is tested.
We want families to have teaching they can share.
And we want the message of salvation through Jesus Christ to reach beyond the limits of one post, one page, or one person's voice.
But continuing and expanding this work requires real support.
You do not have to pay to glorify Jesus.
And you should never feel that your financial circumstances make you less valuable to this community.
It is the opportunity to participate in a mission that points people beyond themselves and toward the Savior.
But only Jesus Christ can save a soul.
That distinction must never be lost.
Before you leave, I want you to imagine something.
Imagine standing before the Lord one day.
The memories of those who wounded you no longer rule your heart.
The unfinished arguments no longer demand another hearing.
The hunger for revenge has finally lost its voice.
Not because evil was insignificant.
Not because justice was abandoned.
But because you are standing before the righteous Savior who knows every truth, judges with perfect justice, and makes all things new.
And in His presence, the thing that once seemed impossible to surrender no longer owns you.
Perhaps that work of surrender can begin today.
Not when your enemy apologizes.
Not when they suffer.
Not when they finally understand your pain.
Today.
You can bring the wound to Jesus.
You can repent of the revenge you have cherished.
You can ask for grace to respond truthfully and wisely.
You can take the necessary steps to protect yourself and others.
You can trust that the Lord sees what you cannot resolve.
And you can remember that the One who calls you to overcome evil with good is the very One who has already conquered sin and death through His cross and resurrection.
So no, Romans 12:20 is not Jesus teaching you how to hurt someone through kindness.
It is Scripture calling you away from vengeance and toward the kind of goodness that refuses to become another form of evil.
The burning coals are not yours to weaponize.
The judgment is not yours to control.
The repentance of another person is not yours to manufacture.
But your heart can be surrendered to Christ.
And His grace is sufficient for the journey of obedience that follows.
Because the greatest miracle may not be watching the person who hurt you finally burn with regret—but watching Jesus remove the hatred that was slowly burning you alive.
